newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany insists Kohl invited Belo for rights talks.
newsitem.headline: Germany insists Kohl invited Belo for rights talks.

text.p: Germany insisted on Tuesday that East Timorese Nobel Peace Prize laureate Bishop Carlos Belo had not snubbed Chancellor Helmut Kohl when he declined to meet him to talk about human rights during his visit to Indonesia.

Deputy government spokesman Herbert Schmuelling said in Bonn that Belo, who told Reuters in Jakarta he had not been officially invited to meet Kohl, had sent a message saying he regretted not being able to meet the chancellor.
"He also expressed his hope that he could meet the chancellor on the occasion of his trip in December to Oslo (to receive the Nobel Prize)," he said.

Kohl, criticised at home for playing down human rights on his trip to Indonesia this week, hastily tried to have Belo flown to Jakarta on Monday to join other church leaders he met after his talks with Indonesian President Suharto.
The chancellor said Belo, awarded the prize for his work in the troubled territory of East Timor that Indonesia annexed in 1975, had bowed out because of pressing pastoral duties.
The bishop later told Reuters he had never received an invitation but would have been too busy anyway.
"The Nobel Peace Prize winner Bishop Carlos Belo was invited to meet the chancellor in Jakarta in several different ways," Schmuelling said in a statement issued in Bonn.

He said Bonn's ambassador in Jakarta, the papal nuntius there and Belo's Salesian order had all tried to arrange the meeting. Germany even offered to fly him from the East Timor capital of Dili to Jakarta.
"Bishop Belo sent the chancellor a letter via the German ambassador on October 28 saying he unfortunately could not take up the invitation because of urgent pastoral work," he said.
Belo was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize early this month with self-exiled East Timorese resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta, who had called on Kohl to raise the East Timor issue with Suharto.

Indonesian troops invaded East Timor in December 1975 and Jakarta declared it Indonesia's 27th province the following year. The United Nations has never recognised the move and still regards the former colonial ruler Portugal as the administering power.
